sources.text notes:
Instruction cycle (fetch-decode-execute)
- The CPU repeats this cycle from boot-up until shutdown to process instructions.
- Three main stages: fetch, decode and execute.
- Simple CPUs finish one instruction before starting the next; modern CPUs overlap the stages using an instruction pipeline.
sources.audio transcript: In this part of the lecture we will walk through the fetch stage, which is the same for every instruction. The program counter contains the address of the instruction to be fetched. This addresses copied to the memory address register. The control unit then sends a signal on the control bus to read memory at that address, and the data is placed on the data bus. The instruction is loaded into the memory data register, and at this point the program counter is incremented by one. Finally, the contents of the memory data register are copied into the current instruction register, where the opcode and the operand can be decoded, in the decode stage the control unit interprets the instruction, and in the execute stage the arithmetic logic unit carries out the operation.
sources.slide text:
Registers in the instruction cycle
Program counter (PC): address of the next instruction
Memory address register (MAR): address being read or written
Memory data register (MDR): data read from or written to
memory
Current instruction register (CIR): instruction being decoded

pack.summary: The instruction cycle consists of three stages: fetch, decode, and execute. The CPU repeats this cycle to process instructions.

key_concepts.explanation: The CPU repeats the instruction cycle to process instructions.
The program counter contains the address of the instruction to be fetched.
The control unit interprets the instruction in the decode stage.
The arithmetic logic unit carries out the operation in the execute stage.
Registers are used to store data during the instruction cycle.
